accuracy.evidence: Checked against the CASEL framework (self-awareness: recognising one's own patterns and strengths; relationship skills) and the PSHE Association KS2 programme of study (Relationships: recognise what makes a positive friendship, reflect on own behaviour, strategies to manage friendships). Goal framing follows Gollwitzer's implementation intentions (when X, I will Y); the strengths-plus-stretches framing avoids fault-only self-criticism, consistent with self-compassion research.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips children make when they reflect: treating one incident as a pattern (predict: picked the game once), labelling the whole self (Kai is a bad person, I am bossy), fault-only reflection (predict on honest reflection), swinging to the opposite extreme (Never suggest a game again, always argue back), blaming the other person, boasting as a strength, and vague goals (Be nicer, Be braver).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmirror is new: a tally board where six first-person moments are dragged into three columns until the tallest column shows the pattern, a never-to-always habit slider whose friend speech bubble changes live with the amount, a strength-or-stretch mirror sort, and a goal slot fed by pattern cards. No other lab tallies the learner's own week or uses a dose slider for social habits.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step is one idea of the topic in order: a pattern is what happens most (tally 3 of 6 deciding moments), habits help in the right amount (three sliders all succeed only in the middle zone, with friends saying why both ends hurt), fair reflection names strengths and stretches (3 and 3), and a pattern becomes a checkable when + I will goal that keeps the strength.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions are each answered by the following task: once versus again-and-again before tallying, leading as always good versus the right amount before the slider, faults-only versus strengths and stretches before the mirror sort, and the vague be a better friend versus a lunch-time question goal before choosing goals.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge items rotate answer order and every wrong option is tagged (harsh, blame, once, label, vague, extreme, always, brag) with its own why message, e.g. That judges the whole person. Name the action, so it can change. Lab misses explain the specific card, e.g. Walking off leaves the problem there, and the slider repeats the friend's reaction.

readability.evidence: Learner text scores about FK grade 3 and the adult text about FK 8.0, inside the learner targets. Lab sentences are short and concrete with named children (Kai, Ava, Leo, Priya, Jo, Mo), playground and lunch contexts, and age-fit words: pattern, strength, stretch, goal, right amount, with no jargon in kid-facing lines.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries one teachable idea: your own part, patterns versus moments, right-amount habits, strengths plus one stretch with a worked goal. The adult text names standards, the three core ideas, a common mistakes list, and the lab sequence. Items use parameterised tallies and day counts tied to reflection, not unrelated arithmetic.

mobile.evidence: Checked at iPhone 13 (390px) light and Android 360px dark: three tally columns, the slider and the goal cards fit without clipping, card text wraps inside its plate, and the tap-a-column, Less/More/Check and goal buttons wrap below the canvas as large tap targets so no drag is required.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (column buttons, Strength/Stretch, Less/More/Check, goal buttons); the canvas aria-label and live status speak each card, slider value out of 10 and friend reaction; axe ran clean in both themes; colour is never the only signal because every state also has a text or emoji cue.
